# How the communities see it {#sec-communities}

Gridded data is handled by several communities that grew up separately.
Each has a default answer to the two questions, built into its formats and
its software, and each default is right for the work that community mostly
does. This chapter describes each view in its own terms first, then puts
them side by side.

## Remote sensing and GIS

**Typical tools:** GDAL's classic raster model, GeoTIFF and COG, terra,
rasterio, QGIS.

The working model here is that an image starts raw and ends rectified. A
sensor captures pixels with messy geometry; ground control points, rational
polynomial coefficients or geolocation arrays describe that geometry; the
data is warped onto a map grid; the map grid is the product. The affine
geotransform describes the finished state, so a "proper" raster is a
regular grid with six numbers and a CRS. Anything else is an intermediate
form waiting to be corrected.

The answer to question one is therefore "regular, or not yet". The answer
to question two is "whatever CRS the geotransform is in", carried as a full
CRS definition.

**What this view gets right:** it never stores a regular grid expensively,
it carries the frame, and it has two decades of warping machinery for
turning anything into a regular grid.

**Where it struggles:** it has one slot for "not regular", the geolocation
array, which lumps together a sensor swath, an ocean model's tripolar grid
and a projected grid written out as longitude and latitude. It cannot tell
case E from case H in @tbl-costumes without help. It also tends to reject
frames it did not expect: GDAL's classic netCDF reader will not accept
rotated-pole axes as x and y by default (@sec-case-cordex).

## Climate and ocean modelling

**Typical tools:** netCDF and the CF conventions, CDO, NCO, ESMF, xarray.

A model runs on a computational grid, writes output on that grid, and the
grid *is* the coordinate system. A NEMO modeller with 2D `nav_lon` and
`nav_lat` arrays is not thinking "this needs rectification". Those arrays
describe where every cell is, completely, and regridding to something else
is an analytical choice with explicit methods (bilinear, conservative,
nearest neighbour), not a correction. That is why there is no
"warp on read" in this world and why nobody in it talks about
rectification.

CF encodes the answer to question one through the shape of coordinate
variables: 1D coordinate variables named after their dimension for regular
and rectilinear grids, 2D auxiliary coordinate variables listed in a
`coordinates` attribute for curvilinear ones. Question two is answered by a
`grid_mapping` variable, added later in CF's history and often treated as
optional, with `crs_wkt` added in CF 1.7 as a supplement.

**What this view gets right:** coordinate arrays are the honest description
of grids that really are curvilinear, which most model grids near the poles
are. It keeps the native grid authoritative.

**Where it struggles:** it reads geometry from storage shape, so a
regular grid stored as 2D arrays is labelled curvilinear. It stores regular
grids as coordinate arrays by default (case C). The frame is often missing
or broken, because a file with good longitude and latitude arrays still
"works" without it. In the MAR CORDEX file the `grid_mapping` attribute
pointed at a variable name that did not exist; nothing warned.

## Array computing

**Typical tools:** NumPy, xarray's core data model, Zarr, VirtualiZarr and
icechunk.

Here an array has named dimensions, which are axes, and coordinates, which
are labels attached to those axes. A coordinate is just a value per
position. Geography is not special: latitude, depth, time and ensemble
member are all coordinates.

This view gives question one a natural home (1D coordinates on one
dimension, 2D coordinates on two) and question two none at all; a CRS is
metadata some other layer may interpret. Until 2025, xarray had no way to
represent "this coordinate is regular" except by materialising every value.
Recent releases added `RangeIndex` and a general `CoordinateTransformIndex`,
and the rasterix package builds an affine `RasterIndex` on it, so a regular
grid can now be held as a transform.

**What this view gets right:** uniform handling of every dimension, lazy
computation, and a clean separation between data and labels.

**Where it struggles:** the frame does not travel with the coordinates
unless something makes it. In Earthmover's icechunk copy of GOES-16, the
scan-angle coordinates were carried faithfully across four time partitions,
and the geostationary projection needed to interpret them was not
(@sec-case-goes). The word "dimension" also means something different here
than in geometry (@sec-two-questions).

## Scientific visualisation and computational fluid dynamics

**Typical tools:** VTK, ParaView, the grid taxonomies taught with them.

This community gave us the cleanest version of the ladder. VTK has a data
type per rung: image data (uniform), rectilinear grid, structured grid
(curvilinear), unstructured grid. The distinction is entirely about how
positions are stored: implicitly, semi-implicitly, or explicitly.

**What this view gets right:** it separates index structure from position
completely, and its vocabulary is precise.

**Where it struggles:** there is no CRS. Positions are numbers in one
Cartesian space, so the question "regular in what?" never arises. Imported
into geoscience, the taxonomy is applied to whatever coordinates the file
happens to store, which is how a polar stereographic grid stored as
longitude and latitude becomes "structured" rather than "image data".

## Meshes and global grid systems

**Typical tools:** UGRID, H3, S2, HEALPix, triangulation libraries.

This view starts from the surface of the Earth instead of from an array. If
the sphere comes first, a grid's job is to cover it sensibly: correct
adjacency across the antimeridian, no thousands of redundant cells at the
pole, often equal area. The row and column index is given up, deliberately.

**Where it meets this book:** the ladder is silent about the manifold, and
these systems exist because some problems need the manifold built in
(@sec-edges). The same confusion also appears in meshes: triangulating
longitude and latitude as if they were planar x and y is the mesh version
of treating a frame as if it were geometry.

## Plotting

**Typical tools:** base R `image()` and `rasterImage()`, matplotlib
`imshow()` and `pcolormesh()`, cartopy.

Plotting libraries embody the ladder without naming it. `rasterImage()` and
`imshow(extent=...)` take an image and a bounding box: a regular grid.
`image()` takes coordinate vectors: a rectilinear grid, with edges or
centres. `pcolormesh()` takes 1D or 2D coordinates and draws quadrilaterals:
rectilinear or curvilinear. They answer question one by their argument
types, ignore question two, and are a common source of the half-pixel
confusion between edges and centres.

## Side by side

| Community | Default unit of truth | Question one comes from | Question two comes from | Typical blind spot |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Remote sensing, GIS | affine transform | is there a geotransform? | full CRS on the dataset | one bucket for every non-affine grid; unfamiliar frames rejected |
| Climate, ocean modelling | coordinate arrays | shape of coordinate variables | optional `grid_mapping` | storage shape read as geometry; frame often missing |
| Array computing | labelled axes | 1D or 2D coordinates | not modelled | frame does not travel with coordinates |
| Scientific visualisation | storage type | data type | none | no notion of frame |
| Meshes, DGGS | cells on the sphere | explicit topology | built into the cell scheme | lon/lat treated as planar in meshes |
| Plotting | function signature | argument types | external (cartopy, map projections) | edges vs centres |

: How each community answers the two questions. {#tbl-communities}

Read across a row and each view is coherent. Read down a column and the
problem appears: there is no shared answer to either question, and nothing
in the data says which community wrote it. The next chapter shows what the
software built by these communities actually does with the same files.
